title: Current engagement with unreliable sites from web search driven by navigational search (Greene, Pisharody, Meyer, Pereira, Dodhia, Lavista Ferres & Shapiro, Science Advances 10, eadn3750, 2024)
screen_reason: Log study of ~14 billion Bing search engine result pages. It reports the share of search results that link to domains rated unreliable by NewsGuard (1.4% and 0.9% in two representative samples) and the share of all engagement with unreliable sites that originates from a small class of queries (>82% from unreliable-site navigational queries, which are 0.88%/1.62% of searches). These meet the CONTENT and CONCENTRATION criteria.

estimates.country: United States (framing: "Bing, the second most popular search engine in the U.S."); samples are English-language queries with no geographic restriction stated
estimates.platform: Bing web search (sample 1: weighted random sample of >100,000 information-seeking queries)
estimates.measure_type: % of Bing search results (top-10 links returned) that linked to a domain rated unreliable by NewsGuard, in the volume-weighted sample of heavily searched information-seeking queries
estimates.value_raw: "In sample 1, around 1.4% of SERPs linked to an unreliable news source and 27% to reliable news sites."
estimates.denominator: roughly 12.6 billion SERPs (top-10 result URLs per search) returned June-August 2022 for a weighted random sample of more than 100,000 information-seeking English queries on Bing (bots and adult queries removed)
estimates.definition: Result URL truncated to its second-level domain and matched to NewsGuard: a domain scoring below 60 of 100 counts as an unreliable information source
estimates.misinfo_def: "Sites that receive an overall score that falls below 60 of 100 are classified as unreliable information sources" (NewsGuard ratings based on nine criteria including whether sites publish false content and correct factual errors)
estimates.source_quote: We find that exposure to unreliable sites from Bing is infrequent (Fig. 1). In sample 1, around 1.4% of SERPs linked to an unreliable news source and 27% to reliable news sites.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: NewsGuard ratings of more than 8000 domains (roughly 5000 reliable, 3000 unreliable); results re-estimated with Media Bias/Fact Check (low/very low factual reporting) in the Supplementary Materials with consistent conclusions; "We cannot identify if a specific URL contains unreliable information, only that it comes from a domain that has been rated as an unreliable information source by a third party"
estimates.moderator_quote: From the population of Bing searches, we narrow our potential sample down to information-seeking queries, which we define as the set of queries that led users to any of the more than 8000 domains rated for reliability by NewsGuard ... In both samples, we collect the top 10 search results as few users are likely to engage with content at higher ranks.
estimates.notes: Coded CONTENT because the protocol lists search results among items that exist; note the paper itself calls this 'exposure' and defines exposure as the top-10 URLs presented on a user's screen, so an EXPOSURE reading is arguable. denom_selection=curated because only the first page (top 10 ranks) is counted; denom_scope=news_diet because the query universe is filtered to information-seeking (news-capable) queries rather than all searches. Geographic scope is not explicitly restricted to the US anywhere in the text; the US coding follows the paper's framing.

This sample, collected after the integration of large language models into the search engine, contains roughly 1.1 billion SERPs.
estimates.notes: Separate row from sample 1: different sampling design (unweighted random rather than volume-weighted), different period (2023 vs 2022) and collected after LLM integration into Bing. Same caveats on construct, denom_selection and geography as the sample-1 row.

estimates.country: United States (framing); English-language Bing queries, no geographic restriction stated
estimates.measure_type: Share of all engagement (navigation) with unreliable sites that originates from unreliable-site navigational queries, which are themselves 0.88% of searches
estimates.value_raw: Table 1, Sample 1: "% Total searches 0.88 | % Unreliable exposure 15.37 | % Unreliable engagement 82.21"
estimates.conc_group_label: unreliable-site navigational queries (USNQs): searches for the name of a site rated unreliable, e.g. searching "breitbart"
estimates.denominator: all engagement (clicks/navigations from Bing results) with unreliable sites in sample 1; ~900 million navigation instances were captured across the study
estimates.definition: Queries identified as USNQs (queries that frequently led to the landing page of an unreliable site; identification precision 0.986, recall 0.915) versus all other searches; engagement = navigation to a page presented by the search engine
estimates.misinfo_def: NewsGuard score below 60 of 100 = unreliable information source
estimates.n: sample 1 = ~12.6 billion SERPs; engagement instances not reported separately per sample
estimates.source_quote: Overall, USNQ searches make up a small percent of the total searches, 0.88% in sample 1 and 1.62% in sample 2. ... in sample 2, USNQ searches account for less than 2% of searches, yet more than 82% of the engagement with unreliable sites originate from a USNQ search (Table 1).
estimates.ground_truth_detail: NewsGuard domain ratings; USNQ identification validated against domain experts (precision = 0.986, recall = 0.915)
estimates.moderator_quote: Table 1. Descriptive information on the occurrence of USNQ searches. % Total searches indicates the percentage of total search results that are USNQ searches. ... % Unreliable engagement indicates the percentage of total engagement with unreliable sites originating from USNQ searches.
estimates.notes: Borderline because the concentrating group is a class of QUERIES, not users or sources, so conc_unit (user|source) does not apply and is left empty; conc_dimension coded 'exposure' because engagement here means clicks/navigations, not resharing. Caution: the running text (p. 3) states that 46.98% of unreliable exposure comes from USNQs in sample 1 and 15.37% in sample 2, which is the reverse of Table 1; Table 1 is used here for the exposure figure quoted in the value_raw, and the 82% engagement figure is consistent between text and table for both samples.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: (i) rank-truncated variants - 'around 1.2% of the top 3 results link to unreliable information sites' in both samples (vs 1.4% and 0.9% overall) - these are subsets of the same measure; (ii) the conditional engagement probabilities by query type (sample 1: 0.926 for USNQ vs 0.003 for non-USNQ; sample 2: 0.870 vs 0.004) and the exposure multipliers (20x and 54x), which are query-type subgroup contrasts rather than the study's headline prevalence; (iii) 'For non-USNQ searches, less than 1% of the results at rank 1 were unreliable sites, while this value was around 90% for USNQ searches' - rank-1 subgroup values, the first of which is a bound rather than a point estimate; (iv) the reliable-site shares (27%, 41%, 28%, 43%), which are not misinformation; (v) the MBFC robustness re-estimates, which are in the Supplementary Materials and not in this text. The overall share of ~900 million engagement instances that went to unreliable sites is never stated as a percentage in the main text.

rob.design: Two large random samples of anonymised Bing logs: sample 1 = all top-10 results returned June-August 2022 for a volume-weighted random sample of >100,000 information-seeking English queries (~12.6 billion SERPs); sample 2 = simple random sample of information-seeking English search results April-June 2023 (~1.1 billion SERPs); bots and adult queries excluded; engagement measured as navigation from a presented link (~900 million instances). Domain-level reliability from NewsGuard (<60/100), with Media Bias/Fact Check as a robustness check; USNQ identification validated by domain experts (precision 0.986, recall 0.915). Limitations acknowledged: one search engine, domain-level rather than URL-level classification, no individual-level tracking, topical domains may vary. One internal inconsistency: the text and Table 1 swap the sample-1 and sample-2 unreliable-exposure shares (15.37% vs 46.98%).
rob.item6_quote: Sites that receive an overall score that falls below 60 of 100 are classified as unreliable information sources. Domains with a score of 60 or greater are classified as reliable information sources.
rob.item10_quote: In sample 1, around 1.4% of SERPs linked to an unreliable news source and 27% to reliable news sites. In sample 2, around 0.9% of SERPs linked to an unreliable news source and 41% to a reliable news site.
